Miguel’s Three Things to Use Tomorrow

One classroom routine, one ready resource, and one professional practice.
Presenter: Miguel Guhlin
Three quick wins, about 60 seconds each
For educators and instructional coaches
✦ Miguel’s Three ThingsPresenter: Miguel Guhlinmguhlin.org · tcea.org

I am keeping this short on purpose. This is not a full workshop or a catalog tour. It is a quick sampler: one routine, one ready resource, and one professional practice that a teacher could try tomorrow. Each idea gets a fast explanation, a practical use case, and a link to come back to later. The goal is simple: leave with one thing worth trying, not a dozen links you feel guilty about never opening.

✦ Miguel’s Three ThingsPresenter: Miguel Guhlinmguhlin.org · tcea.org

The format matters because choice overload is real. I do not want this to feel like another list of tools, sites, and clever ideas that teachers have to chase later. The three choices serve different needs. ACE helps with daily checking for understanding. CTOBs help when you need a ready activity that makes students reason from evidence. The study kit prompt helps during planning. I would frame this as a small menu, then ask people to choose the one that solves a real problem they already have.

Thing one · classroom routine

ACE makes thinking visible

Ask students to show ownership of an idea in three short moves.
A

Articulate

Say it in your own words. Use a real example.

C

Connect

Link it to something you already know. Explain why.

E

Extend

Use it in a new situation. Try a problem nobody handed you.

Tomorrow move: Use ACE as a three-line exit ticket after one concept you already planned to teach.
✦ Miguel’s Three ThingsPresenter: Miguel Guhlinmguhlin.org · tcea.org

ACE is useful because it gets past the polish of the product. A student can turn in something neat and still not own the idea. Articulate asks for the idea in the student’s own words. Connect asks the student to explain how the idea fits with something else. Extend asks the student to apply it somewhere new. Tomorrow, this does not need a special handout. Ask for three lines on paper, in a notebook, or in a shared document, and listen for where the thinking breaks down.

Make it a routine

Run ACE in 30 seconds

Keep it light enough that students will actually do it.
1

Ask one idea

Do not ACE the whole lesson. Choose the concept that matters most.

What is this in your own words?
2

Listen for the gap

Look for missing vocabulary, weak links, or a copied explanation.

How does this connect?
3

Decide the next move

Reteach, regroup, extend, or ask for a stronger example.

Where else could you use it?
Tomorrow move: Try ACE out loud while conferring with one student before assigning it to the whole class.
✦ Miguel’s Three ThingsPresenter: Miguel Guhlinmguhlin.org · tcea.org

The trick is to keep ACE small. If we turn it into a worksheet with too many boxes, it stops being a routine and becomes one more thing to grade. I would model it with one concept and one quick answer. Then I would use it during conferring before making it a classwide exit ticket. The teacher is listening for the stage that needs support. Can the student explain it? Can the student connect it? Can the student transfer it? That tells you what to do next.

Thing two · ready resource

CTOBs turn clues into reasoning

Focus on the evidence students use to reach the lock.

Read closely

Students slow down because the clues matter.

Use evidence

Teams have to prove the answer instead of guessing the code.

Explain the thinking

A short debrief turns the activity into a reasoning check.

Tomorrow move: Run one breakout for 10 to 15 minutes. Require evidence for one answer.
✦ Miguel’s Three ThingsPresenter: Miguel Guhlinmguhlin.org · tcea.org

The second item is the ready resource. Critical Thinking Online Breakouts are useful because they do not require a long setup. Students read clues, make choices, and defend their answers. I would connect that to CLEAR because it gives students a clean thinking path: make the claim, check the lens, find the evidence, consider alternatives, and respond. The lock is the hook, but the learning is in the explanation. If there is time for only one follow-up, ask, “What clue proved your answer?”

Thing three · professional practice

Build a student-ready study kit

Use Gen AI to draft practice, then verify it before students see it.

Reusable prompt

Act as a [grade level and subject] teacher. Create a student-ready study kit for [topic]. Include: 1. Five key vocabulary terms 2. Three retrieval questions 3. One misconception check 4. One short practice task 5. An answer key for the teacher Keep the reading level appropriate for [grade].

Use the right input

Start with lesson content, standards, or a topic description. Do not paste student names, grades, accommodations, or private classroom records into a public Gen AI tool.

Teacher judgment still owns the final version.
Tomorrow move: Build one study kit, check every answer, then adjust the reading level.
✦ Miguel’s Three ThingsPresenter: Miguel Guhlinmguhlin.org · tcea.org

The third item is a professional practice, not a magic trick. A study kit prompt can save planning time because the output is concrete: vocabulary, retrieval questions, a misconception check, a short task, and an answer key. The caution belongs on the slide because it matters. Use lesson content. Do not paste student information into a public Gen AI tool. Then verify the result. Gen AI can draft the practice, but the teacher still checks the accuracy, reading level, and fit for the class.

Closing question: Which one thing will you try tomorrow, and what evidence will tell you it helped?
✦ Miguel’s Three ThingsPresenter: Miguel Guhlinmguhlin.org · tcea.org

I would close by narrowing the ask. Try ACE if you need a quick check for understanding. Try one CTOB if students need to read and defend answers with evidence. Try the study kit prompt if your planning time is tight and you need usable review practice. The important part is not choosing the “best” item from the deck. The important part is choosing one small move, trying it tomorrow, and looking for evidence that it made student thinking more visible.
